title: Biomechanical Testing of Murine Tendons
protocol: Euthanize a mouse per IACUC-approved procedure.
Remove upper extremity skin and all muscles over the humerus, then disarticulate the elbow and glenohumeral joints.
Carefully remove all connective tissues attached to the humerus.
Perform microcomputed tomography scanning of the entire bone.
Euthanize a mouse per IACUC-approved procedure.
Remove lower extremity skin, disarticulate the Achilles tendon-calcaneus joint, and joints between calcaneus and other foot bones.
Carefully remove all connective tissues attached to the calcaneus.
Perform microcomputed tomography scanning of the entire bone.
Mix agarose powder in ultrapure water.
Microwave the mixture for 1-3 min until the agarose is completely dissolved.
Fill cryotubes up to three-quarters full with agarose.
Let the agarose cool for about 5-10 min.
Insert bone into the agarose gel.
Insert a cryotube with bone into the scanner.
Reconstruct microcomputed tomography scan projection images into cross-section images.
Use recommended parameters for the experimenter’s scanner/software combination.
Create a 3D model and save it into a standard STL format compatible with most 3D printers and rapid prototyping.
Select File > Open to open the dataset.
Open the dialog File > Preferences and select the Advanced tab.
Use the adaptive rendering algorithm to construct 3D models.
Set the locality parameter to 10, defining the distance in pixels to neighboring points for finding object borders.
Minimize tolerance to 0.1 to decrease file size.
Manually select two images as the top and bottom of the volume of interest range on the “Raw Images” page.
Move to the Region of Interest page and manually select a region of interest on a single cross section image.
Highlight the selected region in red, representing the humerus cross-sectional area.
Repeat the previous step every 10–15 cross-section images.
Move to the Binary Selection page and click From Dataset on the histogram menu.
Click Create a 3D Model file menu on the histogram menu to save a 3D model of the bone in STL format.
Refine the mesh to reduce the size of the STL file and ensure compatibility with solid modeling computer-aided design programs.
Import mesh and select all to edit.
Choose Reduce from the toolset Edit.
Select Triangle Budget from the toolset Reduce Target.
Reduce the Tri Count and accept changes.
Resave the newly reduced file in STL format by choosing Export as…
Use a solid modeling computer-aided design program to create a custom-fit model of humerus gripping fixture.
Open the STL format file of the humerus bone in a solid modeling program.
Save the 3D bone object as a part file.
Manually create three anatomically relevant planes (i.e., sagittal, coronal, transverse).
Define the sagittal plane to cut through the supraspinatus tendon attachment at the greater tuberosity.
Ensure that the 3D block contains the sagittal plane as a plane of symmetry.
Add or cut material from the block if needed to achieve symmetry.
Measure dimensions of the bone along each of the three planes (i.e., height, width, length).
Measure the dimensions of the mechanical testing grips where the 3D printed fixture will be attached.
Design a solid block part ensuring each dimension is at least 5 mm greater than the humerus dimensions.
Account for mechanical testing grip constraints to ensure free assembly and disassembly of the fixture.
Create an assembly model with a solid block and either the right or left humerus bone.
Define the orientation of the bone within the block, specifically the angle between tendon and bone.
Ensure the entire bone volume fits inside the block.
Insert the design part (humerus) and mold base (cylinder block) into an interim assembly.
Select the block in the assembly window and click Edit Component from the Assembly toolbar.
Click Insert > Features > Cavity to create a cavity within the block using the humerus as a mold.
Select Uniform Scaling and enter 0% as the value for scaling in all directions.
Suppress the bone part and save the assembly as a part.
Open the part containing the cylinder with the cavity.
Cut the part along the sagittal plane to create two symmetrical components that fit the bone anteriorly and posteriorly.
Create a revolved cut to smooth the mesh geometry of the cavity for the anterior component.
Create a sketch for the cut by emulating the cavity geometry and adding a locational clearance for free assembly and disassembly between the bone and the anterior component.
Modify the posterior component to imitate the cavity geometry, creating a cut that adds clearance as described above for the anterior component.
Make a cut in the transverse plane starting from the top of the posterior component up to the crest of the greater/lesser tubercle.
Create an opening at the tendon attachment with a cut on the posterior component.
Ensure a snug fit between the two components to allow for free assembly and disassembly.
Euthanize a mouse per IACUC-approved procedure.
Position the mouse in a prone position.
Make an incision in the skin from above the elbow of the forepaw towards the shoulder.
Carefully remove the skin with blunt dissection so that the musculature of the shoulder is visible.
Remove the tissue surrounding the humerus until the bone is exposed and can be held securely with forceps.
Hold the humerus with forceps and carefully remove the deltoid and trapezius muscles to expose the coracoacromial arch.
Identify the acromioclavicular joint and carefully separate the clavicle from the acromion with a scalpel blade.
Remove muscle from its scapular attachment using a scalpel blade, taking care not to damage the supraspinatus tendon and its bony attachment.

Detach the humeral head from the glenoid, lacerating the joint capsule and the infraspinatus, subscapularis, and teres minor tendons with a scalpel blade, taking care not to damage the supraspinatus tendon and its bony attachment.
Disarticulate the elbow joint to separate the humerus from the ulna and radius.
Isolate the humerus - supraspinatus tendon - muscle specimen and clean off excess soft tissues on the humerus and humeral head.
Euthanize a mouse per IACUC-approved procedure.
Position the mouse in a prone position.
Remove the skin with blunt dissection so that the musculature around the ankle and knee joints is exposed, taking care not to damage the Achilles tendon and its bony attachment.
Using a scalpel blade, carefully detach the gastrocnemius muscle from its proximal attachments starting at the Achilles tendon-calcaneus attachment.
Disarticulate the calcaneus from adjacent bones carefully.
Isolate and clean the Achilles tendon-calcaneus specimen of excess soft tissues.
Determine the cross-sectional area of the tendon using microcomputed tomography.
Mix agarose powder in ultrapure water and microwave until completely dissolved, swirling periodically.
Fill cryotubes up to three-quarters full with dissolved agarose.
Let the agarose cool for about 5-10 minutes.
Suspend the specimen in the cryotube by inserting the bone upside down, ensuring only the bone is in the agarose gel.
Gently remove muscle from tendon using a scalpel blade after scanning.
Insert the specimen into the 3D-printed fixture without glue or epoxy; the bone should be held in place with a press fit.
Glue the tendon between a folded thin tissue paper and clamp the construct using thin film grips.
Attach the 3D printed fixture with the specimen into testing grips.
Insert the sample and the grips into a testing bath of phosphate buffered saline (PBS) at 37 °C.
Define the gauge length as the distance from the tendon attachment to the upper grip.
Precondition with 5 cycles between 0.05 N and 0.2 N.
Hold for 120 s.
Use a tension to failure of 0.2%/s.
Collect load-deformation data.
Calculate the strain as the displacement relative to the initial gauge length of the tendon.
Calculate the stress as the force divided by the initial tendon cross-sectional area.
If interested in viscoelastic behavior, perform a stress relaxation prior to the tension test to failure.
Use the data to calculate parameters such as A, B, C, tau1, and tau2 from the quasi-linear viscoelastic model.
From the load deformation curve, calculate the stiffness (slope of linear portion of curve).
Calculate the maximum force.
Calculate the work to yield (the area under the curve up to yield force).
Identify the linear portion by choosing a window of points in the load-deformation curve that maximizes the R2 value for a linear least squares regression.
Determine the stiffness as the slope of the linear portion of the load-displacement curve.
Calculate the modulus from the stress-strain curve.
Calculate the strength from the stress-strain curve.
Calculate the resilience from the stress-strain curve.
Define the yield strain using the RANSAC algorithm when y-fit deviates more than 0.5% of expected stress value.
Identify the yield stress corresponding to the yield strain.
Perform a cyclic loading test after tensile testing for fatigue and viscoelastic properties analysis.
Scan the entire bone sample using microcomputed tomography at an energy of 55 kVP, with Al 0.25 filter, and a resolution of 6 μm.
Create a volume-rendered 3D model of the scanned object using a compatible visualization program.
Inspect the 3D object to determine the failure mode and failure site area.
